corridor: The passage narrows until your shoulders touch both walls, then keeps going like it has somewhere to be.
A long, low tunnel runs ahead of you, its ceiling sagging in the middle like an old mattress.
You step into a corridor so straight and so dark that the far end might be ten yards off or a mile.
The tunnel bends just enough that you never quite see where it's going.
A brick-lined channel stretches out in front of you, ankle-deep and sloping gently toward somewhere worse.
The ceiling drops to stooping height and stays there for longer than seems fair.
You come out onto a narrow walkway bolted to the wall, with black water moving slowly underneath.
Old rails run down the middle of this tunnel, and the gravel between them crunches like teeth.
The passage here is wide enough for one person and a lot of pipes, and the pipes got here first.
You duck into a round pipe just tall enough to walk through, if you don't mind walking like a question mark.
A dead escalator carries you nowhere, its steps sloping down into a long, tiled passage.
chamber: The tunnel widens into a chamber somebody once tried, and failed, to keep dry.
The walls fall away and the ceiling climbs out of reach of your light, leaving you in a space too big to see the edges of.
You enter a vaulted hall held up by brick pillars, each one wearing a collar of green slime at knee height.
The room opens out around a concrete pit wide enough to park a bus in, and someone has.
You step onto a long platform with a tiled wall on one side and a drop to the tracks on the other.
A cathedral of pipework rises around you, valves the size of tractor wheels stacked three stories high.
The floor slopes down into a broad, low basin where the water has gone still and opaque.
You walk out into a parking level where the columns go on in rows until the dark eats them.
The space ahead is a huge round tank, big enough that your footsteps take a while to come back.
The passage spills out into a ticket hall the size of a church, its booths dark and its benches bolted down.
You climb down into a vast flooded vault where the pillars stand in the water like the legs of something enormous.
small: You squeeze into a room roughly the size of a walk-in closet, which it was.
The door gives onto a cramped little room where the ceiling is close and the air is closer.
You step into a chain-link cage bolted to the wall, its door hanging from one hinge.
This is a utility room, square and windowless, built for one bored technician at a time.
You enter a small, low room where every surface has a dial, a switch, or a warning label.
A narrow side room opens off the passage, barely deep enough to turn around in.
The room is tiny, tiled, and much too warm, like the inside of a mouth.
You shoulder open a door into a closet that smells of floor wax and is barely bigger than the mop inside it.
The room is a squat concrete box with one bulb, one chair, and no good reason to exist.

sights: Brown tide lines climb the walls, each one a little higher than the last.
A shopping cart lies on its side, full of wet newspaper that has fused into one gray brick.
Someone has spray-painted an arrow on the wall pointing back the way you came. Underneath it says NOPE.
A row of lockers stands open and empty, except for one, which is padlocked and dented from the inside.
Tree roots have punched through the ceiling and hang down in pale bundles, still dripping.
A single rain boot stands upright in the middle of the floor, perfectly placed, as if waiting for its foot.
The emergency lights still work, one in three of them, and the ones that do are red.
A subway map is bolted to the wall, its lines rerouted in marker to stations that don't exist.
A pile of bones sits neatly in the corner, sorted by size.
A car sits up to its windows in black water. Its hazard lights are still blinking.
Fat white mushrooms grow in a ring around a drain grate, as though they're guarding it.
A wall of electrical meters spins in unison, measuring something that isn't electricity.
Somebody left a sleeping bag here, zipped all the way shut, and you decide not to check.
Coins carpet the floor around a dead fountain, every one of them gone green.
A rusted ladder climbs to a manhole cover that has been welded shut from above.
Thousands of plastic bottles have washed up against a grate and formed a glittering, crackling dam.
A fire hose hangs from its reel, unspooled, running off into the dark like it's still trying to reach something.
Chalk tally marks cover one wall from floor to ceiling, and the last few rows get very shaky.
A wedding dress hangs from a pipe, gray with mold, its hem chewed into a second kind of lace.
A bank of washing machines lines the wall, and one of them is still churning something heavy.
A turnstile stands alone in the middle of the room, attached to no wall at all.
Something has gnawed every cable along the ceiling down to bright, bare copper.
A maintenance cart sits abandoned with its toolbox open, every tool gone except one bent spoon.
Water pours from a cracked pipe in a smooth, glassy sheet, and the wall behind it is covered in handprints.
An office chair is bolted to the ceiling upside down, with a coffee mug duct-taped to the armrest.
A slick of oil on the water makes rainbows that drift against the current.
Rows of dead fluorescent tubes hang on chains, swaying slightly, though there's no breeze.
A vending machine lies face-down on the floor like it fainted.
Rat-sized holes riddle the bottom of the wall in a pattern too regular to be an accident.
A pallet of canned beans has burst open, and every single can is bulging.
A painted sign reads FLOOD LEVEL 1972, and the water line is a foot above it.
A shed snakeskin as thick as a fire hose is draped over the railing.
Dozens of shoes, no two a pair, are lined up along the wall heel to toe.
A security camera on the wall swivels to follow you, its little light blinking green.
Cracked floor tiles spell out the name of a station, most of the letters long since washed away.
A janitor's mop bucket stands full of water so clean and clear it looks wrong down here.
An apartment buzzer panel is mounted on bare concrete with no building above it. One button is worn smooth.
A great iron wheel valve is chained shut, with a handwritten note taped to it that just says DON'T.
Garbage bags are stacked to the ceiling in one corner, and the bottom row rises and falls, very slightly.
A payphone hangs on the wall, its receiver off the hook and swinging gently.
A row of payment kiosks blinks PLEASE INSERT CARD at nobody, over and over.
Someone has stacked traffic cones into a careful pyramid, and the top one has a face drawn on it.
sounds: Something behind the pipes drips with no rhythm at all, which is worse than a rhythm.
Far off, a train horn sounds, though nothing has run on these tracks in years.
The pipes knock three times, pause, and knock three times again.
Water gurgles in a drain close by, like a throat clearing.
A fluorescent tube buzzes overhead and flickers in time with your heartbeat.
Somewhere far above, muffled by tons of concrete, a car alarm goes off and never stops.
The room is silent except for a faint ticking, like an engine cooling down.
Something drags slowly across the floor of the next room, then stops when you stop.
Wind moans through a grate in one long, low note that almost sounds like a word.
You hear distant splashing, steady and patient, the sound of something wading.
The concrete creaks under some vast, slow weight, the way a ship's hull complains at sea.
Every drop of water here lands with a tiny metallic ping, like loose change.
A radio somewhere plays static, and every so often the static laughs.
Rats chatter inside the walls, then all go quiet at once.
A pump thrums somewhere deep below, so low you feel it in your fillings more than hear it.
Your footsteps echo back half a second late, and one time too many.
Steam hisses from a valve in short bursts, like something trying to get your attention.
A phone rings once in another room and doesn't ring again.
The water around your ankles makes small sucking sounds whenever you shift your weight.
A heavy door swings slowly on its hinges somewhere close, squealing in a key nobody uses.
Grit trickles down from the ceiling in small, nervous showers.
Something wet slaps against stone, once, a long way off.
The silence is so complete you can hear the blood moving in your ears.
A metal grate rattles in its frame, though nothing is touching it.
Faint music drifts out of a vent, an elevator tune with half its notes missing.
A toilet flushes somewhere in the dark, and it is the most frightening thing you've heard all day.
Far down the tunnel, a recorded voice announces the next stop, then cuts out mid-word.
smells: Smells like a wet dog that works in a copper mine.
The air tastes of rust, the way your mouth does after a nosebleed.
It smells like a basement that has been holding its breath for forty years.
Old motor oil and standing water: the smell of a garage after a flood.
Mildew hangs thick in the air, sweet and furry, like a gym bag left in a hot car.
It smells of hot dust and burnt wiring, the scent of a machine dying slowly.
Wet concrete and lime, cold enough to feel in your sinuses.
The sewer stink hits you like a slap, then settles in like it pays rent.
Bleach, a lot of it, poured by someone trying very hard to cover up something else.
It smells like pennies and pond water.
A sharp chemical tang fills the air, like a swimming pool built over a battery factory.
Diesel exhaust, faint and old, soaked into the walls by decades of trains.
The room smells like rotten eggs and wet matches.
Damp cardboard and mouse droppings, the perfume of every storage unit ever rented.
The air is warm, wet and faintly meaty, like breath.
It smells of grease, the burnt-on black kind from the back of a fryer.
Stagnant water with something green blooming in it, rich and swampy.
Ozone prickles your nose, the smell right before lightning strikes.
It smells like a laundromat, clean and soapy, which down here is deeply suspicious.
Coal smoke and wet brick, like an old city in the rain.
The air reeks of ammonia so sharp it makes your eyes water.
It smells like the inside of an old thermos.
Rust and rot in equal measure, like the hold of a ship.
Someone's cheap cologne lingers here, fresh, and there is nobody in sight to be wearing it.
Nothing. The air smells of absolutely nothing, which is the most unsettling thing yet.
Hot pretzels and bus exhaust, the ghost of a subway concourse at rush hour.
It smells like the bottom of a fish tank nobody has cleaned since the fish died.

stairwell: The sign over the door says EXIT in letters that have stopped trying.
A concrete stairwell spirals down past floor numbers that skip from B1 straight to something unreadable.
The stairs going down are dry, swept and well lit, which is the most threatening thing on this floor.
Fresh air rises from the stairwell below, cold and clean and completely untrustworthy.
Someone has painted DOWN on the stairwell door and then, in much smaller letters, sorry.
A freight elevator waits with its gate open and a single button left on the panel: DOWN.
The stairs down are strung with yellow tape and a sign reading AUTHORIZED CRAWLERS ONLY.
safe: The door has a real lock, the lights are steady, and for the first time in hours your shoulders come down from your ears.
A battered sofa, a working kettle and a sign that says NO FIGHTING: the closest thing to mercy down here.
The air in here is dry and warm, and the noises from the tunnels stop at the threshold as if they've been told to.
It's only a break room, but after the tunnels it feels like a cathedral.
Someone has hung a string of fairy lights in here, the only warm color you've seen since you arrived.
The door seals behind you with a hiss, and the silence on this side is the clean kind.
treasure: Something glints in the corner, and for once it isn't an eye.
A chest sits on a little raised platform, lit from above like it's in a shop window.
Soggy cardboard boxes are stacked here, and one of them is much heavier than cardboard has any right to be.
Coins and broken trinkets are heaped in a nest of rags, the hoard of something that no longer needs it.
A lockbox is chained to a pipe, and the chain has rusted much worse than the lock.
A duffel bag lies half-zipped on the floor, something inside it catching your light.
puzzle: A row of valves lines the wall, each stenciled with a number, and none of the numbers are in order.
Strange symbols are scratched into the floor in a ring, and the dust around them hasn't been disturbed.
An old control panel blinks patiently, waiting for an input it clearly expects you to get wrong.
A heavy door blocks the far side. It has no handle, only a keypad and a great many scratch marks.
Light switches cover an entire wall, and only one bulb in the room is wired to any of them.
Three pipes come out of the wall, labeled HOT, COLD and NO, and each one has a tap.
npc: Someone has been living here: a cot, a camp stove, and a hand-lettered sign that says KNOCK FIRST.
A figure sits in the corner, very still, watching you with the patience of someone who has seen a lot of crawlers walk through.
A folding table holds a cash box and a little bell, and the bell is polished.
Someone is humming behind a stack of crates, and the humming stops when you step inside.
A shopping cart piled with junk is parked neatly against the wall under a hand-painted sign that says OPEN.
Someone has set up a lawn chair and a cooler here, and they look up at you like you're late.
empty: There's nothing else here, and the nothing feels deliberate.
The room is empty and swept clean, as if it's waiting for a delivery.
Nothing in here but water and echoes.
Whatever was in this room has been taken, right down to the screws in the walls.
Bare concrete, nothing else. Even the dust looks like it's thinking about leaving.
Nothing here. Not even rats, and the rats go everywhere.

trapTypes.name: Scald Vent
trapTypes.spotted: The tiles ahead are cleaner than the rest. Boiled clean. You find the vent and wedge it shut with a rag.
trapTypes.triggered: A valve snaps open with a shriek and the corridor fills with live steam.
trapTypes.avoided: A valve snaps open with a shriek. You drop flat and the steam combs over you, close enough to iron your shirt.

trapTypes.name: Rust Spike Grate
trapTypes.spotted: One floor grate sits a half-inch proud of the others. Underneath, something waits with the patience of scrap metal.
trapTypes.triggered: The grate flips and a bed of rusted spikes comes up to meet you like an old friend with knives.
trapTypes.avoided: The grate flips under your heel and you throw yourself sideways as the spikes punch up through empty air.

trapTypes.name: Sump Sinkhole
trapTypes.spotted: The concrete here sags like a stage prop. You skirt the edge and hear the hollow space under it sigh.
trapTypes.triggered: The floor opens like a trapdoor with no opinion about what happens to you next, and you ride the rubble down.
trapTypes.avoided: The floor drops away. You lunge, catch the lip, and haul yourself out with all the grace of laundry.

trapTypes.name: Live Wire
trapTypes.spotted: A cable hangs across the passage at neck height, humming a note you feel in your teeth. You limbo under it with dignity intact.
trapTypes.triggered: The cable kisses your shoulder and every muscle you own files a formal resignation.
trapTypes.avoided: You trace the cable back to a junction box and flip the breaker, feeling briefly like a professional.

trapTypes.name: Gas Pocket
trapTypes.spotted: The air ahead shimmers wrong, and the rats have chewed a detour around this stretch. Smart rats. You follow their route.
trapTypes.triggered: You taste rotten eggs a half-second before the pocket of sewer gas folds around your head like a bag.
trapTypes.avoided: You catch the smell in time, pull your collar over your face, and sprint through the worst of it.

trapTypes.name: Flood Valve
trapTypes.spotted: A tripwire runs to a wheel valve the size of a dinner table. You step over the wire, insulted on its behalf.
trapTypes.triggered: Something clicks, a valve spins, and a wall of black water takes you off your feet and introduces you to the floor.
trapTypes.avoided: Something clicks. You grab a pipe as the water hits, and it only steals your footing and a little of your pride.
